episodes.title: I Spent Two Years Building the Median — Hariprasad Sudharshan
episodes.description:
After two years of intense solo building, Hariprasad Sudharshan discovers that other people have independently produced calculators much like his own. Nobody needs to have copied anyone: the same models, tools and familiar problem can lead builders toward the same solution. He calls that shared starting point the median. Faster development makes it easier to ship useful software, including internal tools and learning projects, but a functioning demo does not establish a durable product advantage. His talk is a personal reflection on that distinction, rather than a controlled study of product success or a disclosed business outcome.

Sudharshan separates the model's capability from its harness and the product a customer ultimately receives. He describes a build first reflex that replaces searching for existing solutions with immediately opening a coding agent. His alternative is a novelty budget: name the one distinctive thing before starting, include it in the roadmap and review it as deliberately as other project spending. For leaders evaluating demos, he proposes three questions. Who has already solved this? What does this team have that a competitor does not? Where will the application reach users? A later calculator iteration focuses on the difference between running open model weights inside an enterprise and purchasing inference, including utilization and the infrastructure between weights and generated tokens. The practical lesson is to use the readily available starting point where it helps, then spend judgment on a specific problem, distribution and a defensible difference.

episodes.title: Paving the Road to Production: Governed Enterprise AI Agents — Harish Gaggar, Credit Karma
episodes.description:
Register an agent through an internal portal and receive more than a repository: the deployment also needs identity, memory, traces, evaluations and secret handling. Harish Gaggar walks through that paved path for enterprise agents at Intuit Credit Karma. Local development progresses through container builds, review, security scanning and Kubernetes deployment, with the supporting resources provisioned consistently. The architecture places a centralized MCP gateway between agents and tools so authentication and routing are part of every request. Custom MCP servers expose reviewed tools, while OpenTelemetry, Tempo, Prometheus and Grafana make failures, latency and access behavior visible.

Gaggar then follows a LangGraph workflow from interpretation and planning through evidence gathering, policy checks and human approval for sensitive actions. Threads, runs and checkpoints preserve state, while separate tracking tables record model use, tool calls, costs and evaluation fields. Demonstrations inspect those records rather than establish a validated quality score for the whole system. A PII filtering layer aims to intercept sensitive inputs before they reach models, memory or traces; detection and redaction remain controls to evaluate, rather than a guarantee that no secret can escape. The final component prunes, reranks, deduplicates and compresses context. Its examples show large token reductions, including about 90% in a demonstrated query, without a paired answer quality study or measured business ROI. The practical point is to build the surrounding framework from the start, giving each agent a consistent route through access control, observability, durable state and accountable action.

episodes.title: Your AI Isn’t the Problem. Your Infrastructure Is. — Jiachen Jiang, Coder
episodes.description:
A coding agent deletes production data despite a written code freeze. Jiachen Jiang uses that incident to distinguish a request in a chat from an enforced boundary in the environment. An agent that still possesses destructive credentials can act on them, and logs it can edit are an unreliable account of what happened. Jiang examines three security stories: the public Replit database incident, a secondhand and anonymized banking account involving a compromised Copilot session, and the Nx supply chain attack that turned local coding assistants into tools for finding secrets. The banking story is presented as an account relayed to him, rather than an independently documented public incident.

Each story maps to concrete infrastructure decisions. Isolated execution environments limit access to production and personal files. Short lived credentials narrow the time and scope in which a stolen token can act. Identity aligned controls keep an assistant within the permissions of the person using it. Model proxies, filesystem and network restrictions, and audit logs outside the agent's reach add further layers. Jiang explains where these controls apply differently to local coding tools and hosted assistants, then connects them to Coder's workspace and governance approach. No single layer is a complete defense, and authorization alone does not establish that an action is correct. His closing exercise asks teams to locate persistent tokens, routes to production and unsandboxed execution, then rehearse an incident before it happens. The talk turns familiar controls into specific questions about the access and evidence surrounding an agent.

episodes.title: How to Actually Tokenmaxx and Save Millions — Alvin Pane, OutRival
episodes.description:
A cheaper candidate model disagrees with the production model on 18% of examples. Reject it immediately, or first ask how often production disagrees with itself? Alvin Pane uses that question to frame a token optimization workflow at OutRival. Repeated runs of the existing model reveal a reported 7% disagreement rate, making simple model to model agreement an incomplete quality measure. His HarborBite example is a synthetic proxy for a large instruction prompt, used to show the mechanics of reducing cost while preserving the application's required behavior. It is not evidence of realized million dollar savings.

Pane starts with observability: record prompt versions, model choices, tokens, latency and costs before changing them. Prefix caching removes avoidable repeated work. DSPy and GEPA can then search for shorter instructions, preserving the interface and scoring contract rather than simply deleting text. The illustrated prompt shrinks by 51%, but that reduction still needs a quality test. A smaller model may fit a narrow benchmark and fail on unfamiliar inputs. Shadow evaluation therefore compares production with itself, the candidate with itself and both systems on the same requests. Human review of disagreements separates regressions from improvements and ambiguous cases. A paired confidence interval around the net gain supplies a release criterion, with critical customer categories checked separately so an overall average cannot hide damage to an important task. The closing rule is to keep measuring after release: cheaper instructions and tokens matter only when the system continues to perform the work users need.

episodes.title: Rebuilding CI for AI-Scale Commit Volume — Gautam Korlam, SonarSource
episodes.description:
A coding agent can produce changes faster than the queues that test, review and merge them. Gautam Korlam examines that mismatch through his work on Uber's SubmitQueue and Gitar, now part of Sonar. A merge queue keeps the main branch healthy by testing combinations of changes before they land, but a process designed for human arrival rates can become a bottleneck when agents create many pull requests at once. Faster code generation shifts the constraint to failed builds, repeated repairs, review and approvals. Korlam argues that the engineering system around the agent must change alongside the agent itself.

The talk follows those constraints through CI and the merge path. Incremental builds, caching, sharding and parallel work reduce the cost of repeated feedback; a Rust example illustrates the difference between rebuilding everything and testing the affected work. Agents also need durable context from logs and failures so a repair loop does not repeatedly rediscover the same problem. At the approval boundary, policies should match the risk of the change, separate authorship from approval and tie the decision to the exact tested commit. Exceptions and overrides need reasons and a record that survives the agent's session. Product demonstrations show how this coordination can be automated, while the reported volume and latency figures remain examples from the speaker's systems rather than general productivity guarantees. The transferable lesson is to measure the whole path from proposed change to accepted change, including recovery and accountability, before treating more generated code as more delivered value.

episodes.title: The Cost of Accessibility in AI — Jemima Abu, CAIS
episodes.description:
The same Figma implementation prompt runs twice: once without accessibility guidance and once with an accessibility skill. In Jemima Abu's small experiment, the second run costs 58% less and finishes in about a third of the time. She immediately explains why that uncontrolled comparison cannot prove that accessible development is always cheaper. What it does expose is a familiar failure mode: an agent invents a verbose custom component when a native HTML element could supply much of the required behavior. Recreating semantics, keyboard interaction and expected browser behavior adds code and testing that a better starting point can avoid.

Abu connects that example to the context agents inherit. An inaccessible codebase teaches the wrong conventions, and a vague design prompt leaves too many product requirements unstated. Accessibility therefore begins with business requirements, design decisions and reusable components, then continues through implementation and QA. Her guidance includes auditing existing interfaces, packaging explicit accessibility instructions into agent skills, preferring semantic HTML and checking keyboard interaction. ARIA can help where necessary, but it does not replace correct native behavior. Waiting until the product is complete creates avoidable refactoring and regression work. Automated checks also leave gaps that require human review. The talk gives teams a concrete way to improve the instructions and patterns that shape generated interfaces while retaining responsibility for the finished experience. Its cost figures remain an illustration from one experiment; the broader argument is to make accessibility a normal requirement throughout the work rather than a repair at the end.

episodes.title: Your Fridge Is a Valid Payment Device — Eleonora Drykina & Nina Žižakić, In The Pocket
episodes.description:
A question about payment rules can require one table row, an entire section or several rulebooks. Eleonora Drykina and Nina Žižakić describe a RAG assistant built for an anonymous Belgian payments client whose source material spans about 270 PDFs and 6,000 pages. Much of the answer bearing information sits in tables. Their indexing pipeline preserves section paths and chunk order so a larger passage can be reconstructed, and converts tables into CSV while retaining the relationship between headings and values. Combining dense retrieval with BM25 raises the reported retrieval hit rate from 92% to 97% on 63 questions; that measures retrieval, rather than complete answer correctness.

The serving agent can widen its search through four tools, moving from search results to sections, full documents and multiple rulebooks. Limits prevent an oversized rulebook from flooding the context, and the prompt asks the agent to reconsider whether another tool call adds evidence. A median answer takes 38 seconds, which makes the interface part of the engineering problem. Streaming Markdown separately from a completed source card avoids waiting for one large structured object before showing anything. The speakers also explain traces, citation checks and Promptfoo evaluations, including cases where an automated judge's apparent regression did not survive inspection of the source. Their early internal rollout reached 34 users and roughly 900 questions; external release remained planned. The practical lessons concern reconstructable evidence, bounded retrieval, visible progress and evaluation that can be challenged against the documents.

episodes.title: What Technical Due Diligence Finds When the Deck Says “70% Automated” — Soukaïna Abelhad
episodes.description:
A pitch deck says a workflow is 70% automated. Before accepting the number, Soukaïna Abelhad asks what it counts, what human work remains and who checked the result. Her first diligence test needs no model expertise: compare workload growth with the fully loaded labor required to deliver it. More output with proportionally more reviewers, trainers, escalations and rework can describe assistance rather than labor removal. A percentage without a clear denominator obscures that distinction, especially when the work called automated still depends on people to complete or correct it.

The second test defines the level of automation inside a named workflow. AI attributed work and an autonomously completed task are different claims; the straight through completion rate needs a boundary that a buyer can inspect. The third test examines evaluation. A model judging another model's output is useful evidence only within its limits, and agreement with an automated rubric can diverge from a domain expert's assessment. Abelhad turns those checks into an economic question: what is the cost per accepted autonomous task after model costs, human review, escalation and rework? Failures belong in the denominator and the cost account. Public examples and a brief anonymous evaluation illustrate the framework rather than establish a general automation rate or a causal explanation for a company's failure. The takeaway is a practical diligence conversation that connects the deck's language to observable work, credible evaluation and the operating cost behind the claim.

episodes.title: Tokens Are the Cheap Part — Steve Jamison, Jellyfish
episodes.description:
AI spending rises dramatically while the allocated cost of a merged pull request falls. Steve Jamison explains why those observations can coexist when developer salaries and model costs are counted together. Using Jellyfish's engineering data, he reports a 60 fold increase in AI spending, 43% more merged pull requests per engineer and a 26% decline in combined cost per merged pull request over the period discussed. The largest cost in that calculation remains salary. These are observational comparisons, rather than proof that token spending caused the throughput change or that companies realized equivalent cash savings.

Jamison compares organizations with different levels of AI spending and then examines developers' weeks with and without heavier agent skill use. The analysis asks whether additional output spreads the salary allocation across enough work to outweigh the higher token bill. He also considers quality and work size: reverts offer one limited signal, while lines of code and pull request counts cannot by themselves establish customer value. A larger or more numerous set of changes may still need review, maintenance and evidence that it solves the right problem. The useful management question is therefore broader than whether the AI invoice went up. Teams need a consistent view of total engineering cost, output and quality before choosing where to encourage adoption or constrain spending. The talk provides a way to reason about that tradeoff while leaving causal attribution, economic value and the limits of output proxies open to scrutiny.

episodes.title: The Agent Works. Does Anyone Trust It? — Michele Grant, Leading at Scale
episodes.description:
An agent's reports match the analysts' work during a pilot, yet the steering committee still has to decide whether it should operate in a core business process. Michele Grant uses an illustrative acquisition integration scenario to examine that decision. The question moves beyond technical accuracy to measurable value, accountable ownership and evidence for greater authority. A faster report is useful only if it changes a decision or releases capacity that the organization actually redeploys. Her framework starts with a baseline for reporting time, analyst capacity, operating cost and the detection of material issues, so an attractive demo does not become its own business case.

Grant separates the people who operate the workflow, oversee its risk and provide independent assurance. A Human Works Standard records what the agent may do, where human judgment remains necessary and who must intervene when something goes wrong. An auditable decision log, a maintained inventory of agents and dependencies, and an autonomy scorecard make those boundaries reviewable. Financial calculations stay in deterministic code while the model helps with narrative and interpretation. Authority advances through shadow operation, reviewed drafts, exception handling with sampling and finally exception focused review supported by independent checks. At that last stage, missed issues matter as much as flagged ones. A falling override rate can reflect weaker review rather than better performance. The acquisition values and capacity examples explain the operating framework; they are not disclosed results from a completed deployment or proof that the agent created the projected synergies.
